content: There is increasing interest in utilizing schools as platforms for immunization and health screening for older children, such as for vaccines like DTP, Td, and the second dose of the measles vaccine. This approach is particularly promising in low-income countries where school enrollment rates are rising. Schools provide an effective setting to integrate vaccine delivery with other health and nutrition interventions aimed at reducing vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs) and improving overall population health. For instance, HPV vaccination can be combined with health education to prevent tobacco use, promote healthy diets to combat obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and provide puberty and menstruation education or iron/folic acid supplements to adolescents. Additionally, linking HPV vaccine delivery with interventions like deworming can enhance coverage and reduce delivery costs. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a School Vaccination Readiness Assessment Tool to evaluate a country’s preparedness for implementing school-based vaccination programs. This tool supports a comprehensive approach to cervical cancer prevention by identifying opportunities for effective interventions across different age groups, based on the natural history of the disease. The Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhea (GAPPD), launched by WHO and UNICEF in 2013, provides an integrated framework of proven interventions to prevent and treat childhood pneumonia and diarrhea. These include vaccines (e.g., pertussis, measles, Hib, pneumococcal conjugate, and rotavirus), handwashing with soap, exclusive breastfeeding for six months, vitamin A supplementation, and appropriate treatment. GAPPD emphasizes the need to integrate activities to maximize benefits and improve efficiency, grouping interventions into three focus areas: protecting children through good health practices, preventing illness through immunization and healthy environments, and treating illnesses with appropriate care. Sudan has made significant progress in introducing new vaccines, such as the rotavirus vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), and the meningitis A vaccine, into its routine immunization program. These efforts have strengthened primary healthcare and equity. However, challenges remain, particularly in data quality and disease surveillance, which are critical for evidence-based solutions. Sudan has implemented a weekly case-based VPD surveillance system and introduced adverse event reporting following immunization. Despite these efforts, conflict has weakened community-based disease surveillance among displaced populations and refugees. The integration of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services into healthcare facilities is also critical. WHO and UNICEF have committed to achieving universal access to WASH in all healthcare facilities by 2030. The WASH FIT tool has been implemented in several countries to assess and improve WASH services, hygiene practices, and risks in healthcare settings. However, more rigorous monitoring and evaluation are needed to sustain these improvements. In Nepal, a novel approach integrated hygiene promotion into routine immunization programs in preparation for the rotavirus vaccine introduction. This initiative demonstrated significant improvements in hygiene behaviors and immunization coverage while reducing vaccine wastage and dropout rates. It also enhanced the capacity of health workers and community health volunteers, with plans for nationwide scaling. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy, launched by WHO and UNICEF, combines prevention and treatment of common childhood illnesses, including immunization. Health workers are trained to assess vaccination status and provide necessary vaccines. The integrated community case management (iCCM) strategy trains community health workers (CHWs) to manage common childhood illnesses and mobilize communities for vaccinations. CHWs assess vaccination status and facilitate immunization for unvaccinated children, particularly in hard-to-reach areas. Tetanus remains a significant public health issue, particularly in low-income regions. Tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines (TTCVs) are included in childhood immunization programs, with booster doses required for long-term immunity. As new vaccines for pregnant women become available, the integration of ANC and immunization will become increasingly important. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is a leading cause of liver cancer and liver disease. WHO recommends that all infants receive the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine (HepB-BD) within 24 hours of birth. However, challenges such as home births and limited health system capacity hinder timely vaccination. Integrating HepB-BD into maternal and newborn care has shown additional benefits, such as early birth registration and improved postnatal care. In India, a project in Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh demonstrated the feasibility of vaccinating newborns with HepB-BD and other vaccines immediately after birth in health facilities. This approach also facilitated early birth registration and follow-up for complete immunization and other services. Postpartum systematic screening using standardized checklists has improved access to family planning, postnatal care, and immunization services. For example, in northern Nigeria, beneficiaries attending immunization and newborn care services were more likely to receive additional health services when systematic screening was implemented.
